A statement, line by line

Source: R/xbrl_lines.R
xbrl_lines.Rd

Returns one statement of every filing in x as it is presented: one row per line, in statement order, with the lines the filer left out derived where they can be. This is what an analysis reads – the fact table is what it is read from.

Usage

xbrl_lines(
  x,
  statement = "balance",
  basis = c("parent", "consolidated"),
  fill = TRUE,
  taxonomy = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A tibble from read_xbrl(). The taxonomy has to be on it: the hierarchy is what names a line the filing never mentioned.

statement

Which statement. "balance", "income", "cashflow" or "equity", or one or more taxonomy statement names for anything else – unique(cvrr_line$statement) lists them.

basis

"parent" (default) or "consolidated". An untagged figure is the parent's, because the taxonomy says so – see add_taxonomy().

fill

Derive the lines the filing left out. Balance sheet only, for the reason above. FALSE returns only what was reported.

taxonomy

Passed to xbrl_fill(). NULL uses the packaged tables.

Value

A tibble in statement order, one row per line per filing: the key – cvr, name, period_start, period_end – then code, elementid, label, value, currency and source, with file last. source is "reported", "derived: identity", or one of xbrl_fill()'s values.

code is the taxonomy's own numbering and sorts into statement order, but it is not an identifier: 861 of 11,809 codes name a different element in a different taxonomy version, and 95 do so within one version. Group a panel on elementid.

Which presentation the filer chose is not your problem

The taxonomy carries the income statement twice, by nature and by function, the balance sheet in three forms, and a dozen sector-specific variants besides. A filing uses one of them and says nothing about the choice. statement = "income" accepts whichever it was. Pass a taxonomy statement name instead of an alias to be exact.

What is derived, and what is not

The balance sheet is a partition: a subtotal is the sum of its parts, so a line the filer omitted can be recovered. Two things do the recovering – five headline identities (Assets = NoncurrentAssets + CurrentAssets and its like), then xbrl_fill() walking the hierarchy – and source says which, on every row.

The income statement is not a partition. It is a cascade: each subtotal is the one above it plus and minus the year's items, and the same figure appears in several steps. Summing components into it would double-count, so fill does nothing outside the balance sheet, and an income statement comes back as reported. check_cascade() is what says whether it reconciles.

Conflicting figures are settled first

A filing can tag the same line twice with different values – the same figure at two precisions, or a nil comparative column. xbrl_resolve() decides between them before anything is derived, because a subtotal derived from the losing reading is worse than a missing one.

See also

xbrl_accounts(), which calls this for both statements at once, xbrl_fill() for the derivation itself, check_statement() and check_cascade() to verify the result adds up.

Other taxonomy: add_taxonomy(), check_breakdown(), check_cascade(), check_continuity(), check_inclusion(), check_movement(), check_statement(), read_taxonomy(), xbrl_accounts(), xbrl_company(), xbrl_fill(), xbrl_movements(), xbrl_note_tables(), xbrl_period(), xbrl_resolve()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")

xbrl_lines(x, "balance")
xbrl_lines(x, "income")

# what the filings did not state, and what it must have been
b <- xbrl_lines(x, "balance")
b[b$source != "reported", ]
} # }
